deviate

DEE-vee-ayt -- built on Latin via, 'road,' so to deviate is literally to leave the road. · verb

What It Means

To deviate is to depart from an established course or plan.

The captain refused to deviate from the charted route, even when the crew begged for a shortcut.

Example

A marching band has rehearsed one formation for weeks, but halfway through the halftime show the drum major suddenly deviates from it, leading everyone into a completely different pattern.

That departure from the rehearsed plan is exactly why deviate fits here. Unlike 'improvise,' which emphasizes inventing something new, deviate emphasizes leaving the set path.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

digress: To digress is to drift away from your topic while speaking or writing -- a storyteller wanders into a side tale, then returns. To deviate is broader and weightier: leaving any established course or plan, from a flight path to a set procedure.

veer: To veer is to swing suddenly in a new direction -- a car veers around a pothole in one sharp motion. To deviate is usually a fuller departure: leaving the established course or plan itself, not just making one quick swerve.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

conform: to follow established rules or patterns

adhere: to stick firmly to a plan or rule

Where it sits · how deliberate and lasting the departure is — stray → deviate → diverge

stray vs. deviate: Stray is a gentler, often accidental version of deviate -- a hiker can stray off a trail without noticing, while deviate usually suggests a more definite departure from a set course.

diverge vs. deviate: Diverge can feel more permanent than deviate: to deviate is to leave an established course, while diverge suggests two paths splitting apart entirely, perhaps never to rejoin.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — de-

prefix — de-: away from, off (Latin)

root — -via-

root — -via-: road, way (Latin (via))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending (Latin (-atus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin deviare combined de- ('off') with via ('road') -- to deviate is literally to step off the road, the same root that gives us viaduct, a roadway carried high across a valley.

Use the root in a new word: viaduct

Use the root in a new word: viaduct: The old stone viaduct carried the railway high above the river valley.
